words.shortDefinition: The fixed-size I/O unit of a database (typically 4–16 KB); all reads and writes move whole units of this size.
words.simpleDefinition: Every time a database reads from or writes to disk, it does so in fixed-size chunks called pages (also called blocks). You cannot read just one row — you must load the entire page containing that row into memory. PostgreSQL uses 8 KB pages; InnoDB uses 16 KB. Every B-tree node, every heap tuple, every WAL record maps to one or more pages.
words.longDefinition: The page is the atomic unit of I/O in every disk-oriented database. This design mirrors hardware realities: spinning disks read and write in sectors (512 B or 4 KB), SSDs erase and program in flash pages, and the OS virtual-memory subsystem works in 4 KB pages. A database page aligns with these units to avoid costly partial-sector reads. Once loaded, a page lives in the buffer pool as a frame of shared memory. All operations — tuple lookups, index traversals, WAL writes — are expressed in whole-page terms. Page size is a critical tuning parameter: larger pages increase the B-tree's fan-out (fewer levels for the same dataset) but waste I/O when only a few rows are needed. PostgreSQL's 8 KB default is compiled in and not runtime-configurable. InnoDB's 16 KB default can be set per tablespace at creation. SQLite allows pages from 512 B to 65 KB. Every page carries a header recording its LSN, a checksum, free-space pointers, and type information — enough metadata for the engine to validate and navigate the page without reading its full content.
words.connector: Think of a page like a page in a physical book — you cannot photocopy just one sentence; you copy the whole page, and the library catalogues books, not sentences.
words.techContext: When diagnosing a query that reads 50 rows but triggers 50 000 I/Os, you are seeing the page as the unit: each row lived on a different page, forcing 50 000 separate disk fetches instead of one sequential scan.
words.exampleSentence: The index lookup needed one row, but the engine loaded the entire 8 KB page containing it into the buffer pool — a page read, not a row read.

codeExample.code:
-- PostgreSQL: inspect page-level details
SELECT * FROM page_header(get_raw_page('orders', 0));
-- Returns: lsn, checksum, flags, lower (end of slot dir),
--          upper (start of tuple area), free space

-- Check page size for the cluster
SHOW block_size;  -- 8192

words.etymology: From Latin pagina ('a leaf of writing'); borrowed directly into database engineering to describe the fixed-size I/O unit, first formalized in IBM's System R papers (1976).

words.shortDefinition: A shared-memory page cache that holds recently read disk pages to avoid repeated disk I/O.
words.simpleDefinition: The buffer pool is the database's RAM cache for disk pages. When the engine needs a page, it checks the buffer pool first. A hit means a nanosecond memory read; a miss means a millisecond disk fetch. The buffer pool is usually the biggest consumer of database process memory and the single most important performance knob — keeping the working set cached is what makes a database fast.
words.longDefinition: The buffer pool is a flat array of fixed-size frames in shared memory, each frame holding exactly one database page. A page table (hash map from page_id to frame index) provides O(1) lookup. Each frame carries a dirty bit (page modified since read), a pin count (active users; pinned pages cannot be evicted), and replacement-policy metadata. When a requested page is not in the pool, the engine must choose a victim frame to evict, optionally writing it back if dirty, then read the new page from disk. The replacement policy — LRU, Clock, LRU-K — determines which frames are selected as victims. PostgreSQL calls its buffer pool shared_buffers (default 128 MB; recommend 25–40% of RAM); InnoDB calls it innodb_buffer_pool_size (recommend 70–80% of RAM). The buffer pool interacts directly with WAL: dirty pages must not be evicted before their corresponding WAL records are flushed — the write-ahead rule. The checkpointer periodically flushes dirty pages to bound crash recovery time, since recovery only needs to replay WAL records written after the last checkpoint.
words.connector: Think of the buffer pool like a librarian's desk — the most-used books stay on the desk (RAM) rather than being returned to the stacks (disk) after every consultation.
words.techContext: A buffer pool hit rate below 95% on a production OLTP system is a warning sign: add RAM, tune shared_buffers, or investigate queries that scan large cold tables and evict hot pages.
words.exampleSentence: After increasing innodb_buffer_pool_size from 4 GB to 12 GB on our read-heavy service, the buffer pool hit rate jumped from 88% to 99.4% and median query latency halved.

codeExample.code:
-- PostgreSQL: buffer pool hit rate
SELECT
  sum(heap_blks_hit)  AS hits,
  sum(heap_blks_read) AS disk_reads,
  round(
    sum(heap_blks_hit)::numeric /
    nullif(sum(heap_blks_hit) + sum(heap_blks_read), 0) * 100, 2
  ) AS hit_rate_pct
FROM pg_statio_user_tables;

words.etymology: Buffer from Latin buffare ('to absorb a blow'); pool in the sense of a shared resource. The term buffer pool was standard in IBM's DB2 documentation and has been the canonical name since the 1970s.

words.shortDefinition: An unordered collection of pages that stores table rows in the order they were inserted.
words.simpleDefinition: A heap file is the simplest table storage format: rows are written to pages in insertion order with no inherent sorting. PostgreSQL stores every table this way; MySQL InnoDB does not (it uses a clustered B+ tree instead). Heap files are simple and fast for inserts but require a full sequential scan or a secondary index to find specific rows.
words.longDefinition: In a heap-organized table, each row (tuple) is assigned a physical address — its CTID in PostgreSQL: a (page_number, slot_number) pair. Rows have no guaranteed order; a freshly deleted row's slot may be reused by a later insert. When a query lacks a usable index, the planner performs a sequential scan reading every page of the heap in file order. PostgreSQL stores each table as a heap file (a fork named after the relation OID), alongside optional visibility map and free space map forks. InnoDB deliberately avoids heap files: every table is stored as a clustered index, physically ordered by primary key. The heap design makes MVCC simpler in PostgreSQL — old tuple versions accumulate in place, and VACUUM reclaims them — but it means every non-primary-key lookup requires traversing a secondary index and then fetching the row from a potentially random heap page. This double-fetch is called a heap fetch or table lookup, and it is why covering indexes are valuable: they eliminate the heap fetch entirely.
words.connector: Think of a heap file like a pile of unsorted papers on a desk — adding new papers is instant (just drop them on top), but finding a specific document means searching through the entire pile unless you have an index.
words.techContext: When PostgreSQL's planner chooses a Seq Scan over an index scan, it has decided that reading every page of the heap sequentially is cheaper than random index-driven heap fetches — true when the query returns a large fraction of rows.
words.exampleSentence: The new secondary index brought query time from 4 seconds to 8 milliseconds by replacing a full heap file scan with an index lookup plus a single heap fetch.

codeExample.code:
-- PostgreSQL: inspect heap file size and page count
SELECT
  pg_size_pretty(pg_relation_size('orders')) AS heap_size,
  pg_relation_size('orders') / 8192          AS page_count;

-- Show CTID (physical address) for rows in the heap
SELECT ctid, order_id FROM orders LIMIT 5;
-- ctid (0,1) means page 0, slot 1

words.etymology: Heap in the computer-science sense of an unordered collection (distinct from the heap data structure); file because it maps to one or more OS files. The term appears in the foundational System R papers and Ramakrishnan & Gehrke's database textbook.

words.shortDefinition: A PostgreSQL optimization that skips index updates when an updated row's new version fits on the same heap page as the old version and no indexed column changed.
words.simpleDefinition: Normally, updating any row in PostgreSQL creates a new row version on any heap page with space, and every index on the table must add a pointer to that new version. A HOT (Heap-Only Tuple) update short-circuits this: if the new version fits on the same heap page as the old version and none of the indexed columns changed, PostgreSQL skips all index updates and instead adds a chain pointer from the old tuple to the new one within the page. Index entries continue pointing to the old tuple, which redirects to the new one at page-scan time.
words.longDefinition: PostgreSQL's MVCC model creates a new physical tuple for every UPDATE — it never modifies a tuple in place. Without optimization, this means every UPDATE on a table with N indexes generates N new index entries (one per index) plus the new heap tuple. For a table with 10 indexes, a single UPDATE touching only non-indexed columns writes 11 items: 1 heap tuple + 10 index entries. HOT (Heap-Only Tuple) optimization eliminates the index writes entirely when two conditions are met: (1) the UPDATE touches no indexed column, and (2) the new tuple version fits on the same heap page as the old version (determined by fillfactor-reserved free space). When both conditions hold, PostgreSQL marks the new tuple with the HEAP_ONLY_TUPLE flag and writes a chain pointer (ctid redirect) from the old tuple to the new tuple — all within the same page. Indexes continue pointing to the old tuple's item pointer, which the heap scan follows to reach the new version. This makes HOT updates write-amplification equivalent to a single-page modification: only the heap page is dirtied, not the index pages. HOT also enables same-page VACUUM: the old dead tuple can be pruned and its space reclaimed during a normal heap page scan (HOT pruning) without a full VACUUM pass touching the index, because no index entry points to the dead tuple. The fill factor setting on a table directly controls HOT eligibility: a lower fill factor (e.g., 70) leaves more free space on each page for HOT chains, increasing the likelihood that updated tuples land on the same page. High-churn tables (frequently updated rows with a stable index column set) benefit most from a low fill factor. HOT was introduced in PostgreSQL 8.3 (2008). Limitations: HOT chains can grow long on heavily updated pages if VACUUM does not run frequently enough; the planner must follow chains during index scans, adding a small per-chain overhead.
words.connector: Think of HOT update like editing a footnote in a printed book: instead of reprinting the entire index with a new page reference, you cross out the footnote in place and write the new text right below it on the same page — anyone following the old index entry just reads the correction directly.
words.techContext: Setting fillfactor=70 on a high-UPDATE table reserves 30% of each page for HOT chains, ensuring most row updates stay on the same page and skip all index maintenance — dramatically reducing write amplification and autovacuum frequency on hot-row tables.
words.exampleSentence: After setting fillfactor=70 on the sessions table and confirming that the indexed user_id column was never updated, the team observed a 65% drop in index write I/O because nearly all updates qualified as HOT and bypassed all five secondary indexes.
words.etymology: HOT is an acronym for Heap-Only Tuple — 'heap-only' because the new tuple version exists only in the heap (the main table storage) and is not referenced by any index entry. Introduced in PostgreSQL 8.3 by Pavan Deolasee and others as a targeted optimization for high-update-rate tables.

words.shortDefinition: PostgreSQL's Generalized Search Tree — an extensible index framework that lets user-defined types plug in their own search predicates and distance functions.
words.simpleDefinition: A GiST index is not one specific tree structure but a framework: you provide four operator class methods (consistent, union, penalty, picksplit) and GiST handles the tree mechanics — node splitting, search traversal, buffering, and concurrency. This extensibility lets a single framework back full-text search (tsvector), geometric containment (PostGIS), range overlap, and nearest-neighbor queries, all using the same B-tree-like page format.
words.longDefinition: B-trees can only answer equality and ordering predicates (=, <, >, BETWEEN) on scalar types. Many useful queries — does this point fall inside this polygon? does this time range overlap that one? what are the 5 nearest restaurants? — require different search semantics that a B-tree cannot express. GiST (Generalized Search Tree) (Hellerstein, Naughton, and Pfeffer, VLDB 1995) provides a generic infrastructure for building balanced, disk-resident, multi-dimensional index trees. Instead of hard-coding split and search logic, GiST delegates to a pluggable operator class that implements four core methods: consistent(entry, query) — does the index node possibly contain results matching query?; union(entries) — compute a bounding predicate that covers all entries in a node; penalty(entry1, entry2) — cost of inserting entry2 into a subtree rooted at entry1 (guides the descent); picksplit(entries) — split a full node into two groups. With these four primitives, GiST implements an R-tree for geometric data, a B+-tree for sorted data, or any other tree variant where the search predicate is monotone (if a predicate is false for a node, it is false for all children). PostgreSQL ships GiST operator classes for: tsvector (full-text search, using query containment as the consistency predicate), geometric types (point, box, circle, polygon — using bounding-box containment), range types (tsrange, numrange — using range overlap), and arrays. PostGIS extends GiST with an R-tree operator class for geography and geometry types, enabling the spatial queries (ST_Intersects, ST_DWithin, KNN) that power mapping applications. GiST also supports nearest-neighbor (KNN) index scans via an optional distance() operator class method: EXPLAIN an ORDER BY ... <-> ... (KNN distance) query and you will see an 'Index Scan using gist_idx ... Order By' node, meaning GiST traverses the tree in distance order rather than scanning all rows. Key trade-off versus GIN: GiST is lossy (consistent() is allowed to return false positives; heap rows must be re-checked), making it faster for spatial/range queries but less suitable for exact set-membership tests where GIN (the inverted index sibling) excels.
words.connector: Think of GiST like a universal remote control with a 'plug-in brain slot': the remote (tree infrastructure) handles all the button mechanics, but you swap in different brains (operator classes) — one brain knows about geography, another about text matching — without rebuilding the hardware.
words.techContext: PostGIS's geometry columns use a GiST index with an R-tree operator class; the ST_DWithin(geom, point, radius) predicate traverses the GiST tree using bounding-box pruning, eliminating the full-table scan that would otherwise be required for proximity queries over millions of locations.
words.exampleSentence: Adding a GiST index on the location column reduced the 'find all stores within 5 km' query from a 4-second full-table scan to a 3 ms index scan, because PostGIS's R-tree operator class pruned 99.8% of bounding boxes before touching the heap.

codeExample.code:
-- PostGIS spatial GiST index
CREATE INDEX idx_stores_location
  ON stores USING gist(location);   -- location is geometry type

-- KNN nearest-neighbor query (uses GiST distance() operator)
SELECT name, ST_Distance(location, ST_MakePoint(-73.99, 40.73)::geography) AS dist_m
FROM stores
ORDER BY location <-> ST_MakePoint(-73.99, 40.73)  -- KNN operator
LIMIT 5;

-- Range overlap GiST index
CREATE INDEX idx_bookings_during
  ON bookings USING gist(during);   -- during is tstzrange

SELECT * FROM bookings
WHERE during && tstzrange('2026-06-12', '2026-06-15');

words.etymology: GiST stands for Generalized Search Tree — 'generalized' because the framework is agnostic to the specific search predicate or data type, making it applicable to any balanced tree structure whose consistency predicate is monotone. Introduced by Hellerstein, Naughton, and Pfeffer at VLDB 1995 and incorporated into PostgreSQL in version 7.0 (2000).

words.shortDefinition: An index using a hash function to map keys to buckets; O(1) point lookups but no range queries.
words.simpleDefinition: A hash index applies a hash function to each indexed key and stores the key-to-row-pointer mapping in hash buckets. Point lookups (equality predicates) are O(1) — compute the hash, go to the bucket. But because hashing destroys the key's sort order, hash indexes cannot answer range queries, prefix matches, or ORDER BY clauses.
words.longDefinition: Hash indexes work by hashing the indexed column value to determine which bucket holds the record's pointer. A lookup for key k computes hash(k), goes directly to that bucket, and either finds the row pointer or confirms absence. This makes equality lookups extremely fast — typically a single I/O in the steady state, versus two to four I/Os for a B-tree traversal. PostgreSQL has supported hash indexes since early versions, but until PostgreSQL 10 they were not WAL-logged and could not survive crash recovery, limiting production use. As of PostgreSQL 10, hash indexes are fully crash-safe. The critical limitation is that the hash function destroys all ordering information. A query for WHERE email = 'alice@example.com' can use a hash index; a query for WHERE created_at BETWEEN '2024-01-01' AND '2024-06-01' cannot. InnoDB does not implement disk-based hash indexes, but it maintains an adaptive hash index in the buffer pool — a read-only cache of recently-accessed B-tree lookups that turns hot repeat lookups into O(1) memory accesses.
words.connector: Think of a hash index like the index in the back of a textbook that lists page numbers for exact terms — fast for 'find exactly this term,' useless for 'find everything between chapter 3 and chapter 5.'
words.techContext: Use a hash index on a high-cardinality equality-only column (UUID primary keys in a lookup table) and save the B-tree for any column that also needs ORDER BY or range predicates.
words.exampleSentence: Switching the session-token lookup from a B-tree to a hash index cut average authentication query time by 40% because the workload is 100% equality lookups and the O(1) bucket fetch beats B-tree traversal.
words.etymology: Hash from German Hackfleisch ('minced meat') via English, referring to chopping data into fixed-size buckets; index from Latin indicare ('to point out'). Hash tables as a data structure were described by Luhn and Dumey in 1954.

words.shortDefinition: An index on a non-primary-key column; in InnoDB it stores the primary key rather than a heap pointer.
words.simpleDefinition: A secondary index lets the database find rows efficiently using a column other than the primary key. In PostgreSQL, secondary index leaves store the heap CTID (page + slot). In InnoDB, they store the primary key value, requiring a second B-tree traversal to fetch the full row. The architectural difference affects query planning and the cost of secondary index lookups.
words.longDefinition: Every index beyond the primary index is a secondary index. Its leaves map the indexed column's value to the row's location. The two major approaches diverge significantly. PostgreSQL's heap-based model stores the physical heap TID (page_number, slot_number) in each leaf. A secondary index lookup is a single B-tree traversal followed by one heap page read. The downside: if a row moves (VACUUM rewrites it to a new location), every secondary index must be updated. InnoDB's clustered model stores the primary key in each secondary index leaf. A secondary index lookup requires two B-tree traversals: secondary index → primary key → primary B-tree for the full row. This double traversal is called a bookmark lookup. The upside: row movements from MVCC updates only require updating the clustered index, not all secondary indexes. Secondary indexes on wide or frequently-updated columns carry substantial write amplification — every row update must update each secondary index covering the changed column.
words.connector: Think of a secondary index like the subject index in a textbook: it points you to a page number (the primary key), and then you go to that page to read the full content.
words.techContext: Before adding a secondary index, estimate write amplification: on a table with 10 secondary indexes, every INSERT requires 11 B-tree leaf insertions — one for the primary key and one for each secondary index.
words.exampleSentence: The secondary index on user_id in the orders table reduced the 'orders for user X' query from a 900 ms full scan to a 2 ms index lookup, at the cost of a second B-tree traversal for each row in InnoDB.
words.etymology: Secondary from Latin secundarius ('of the second rank'); index from Latin indicare ('to point out'). The term secondary index contrasts with the primary (clustered) index, which organises the physical row storage.

words.shortDefinition: An index where the B+ tree leaves ARE the table — rows are stored sorted by the index key.
words.simpleDefinition: In a clustered index, the table's rows are physically stored inside the B+ tree's leaf pages, sorted by the index key. InnoDB always uses a clustered primary key: the leaf pages contain the full rows. PostgreSQL does not have a native clustered index — it stores tables as heaps and keeps indexes separate. Clustered indexes make primary-key lookups and range scans extremely fast.
words.longDefinition: A clustered index (also called an index-organized table) stores the full row at the leaf level of the B+ tree, sorted by the index key. There can be only one clustered index per table because there is only one physical ordering of rows on disk. InnoDB mandates a clustered primary key: if you declare no primary key, InnoDB synthesizes a hidden 6-byte rowid. Every secondary index in InnoDB stores the primary key in its leaves, not a physical pointer — when a row moves due to an update or page split, only the clustered index is rewritten; secondary indexes remain valid. The benefits are: primary-key point lookups require a single B-tree traversal delivering the full row (no second heap read); primary-key range scans read adjacent leaf pages sequentially. The costs: secondary index lookups require a second traversal of the clustered index; random UUID primary keys cause severe page fragmentation and high write amplification because inserts scatter across all leaf pages rather than appending to the right-most leaf.
words.connector: Think of a clustered index like a physical filing cabinet where the folders are sorted by date — finding a folder by date is instant, but keeping them sorted requires inserting new folders at the correct position rather than just dropping them at the back.
words.techContext: InnoDB's requirement for a clustered primary key is why sequential integer or ULID primary keys dramatically outperform random UUID v4 keys: sequential keys always append to the right-most leaf; UUIDs force inserts into random interior pages, causing constant splits.
words.exampleSentence: Switching from UUID v4 to ULID primary keys in InnoDB reduced our peak insert latency by 60% by eliminating the constant mid-tree page splits caused by random key insertion.
words.etymology: Clustered from Latin clustrum ('group, enclosure'), reflecting that rows physically cluster together under their index key. The concept was central to IBM's System R and first implemented in IMS hierarchical databases.

words.pronunciation: WAL (rhymes with pal) or spelled out W-A-L
words.shortDefinition: Write-Ahead Log: every change is written to a sequential log before the data page is modified.
words.simpleDefinition: WAL is the durability primitive of every serious database. Before modifying a page in the buffer pool, the engine appends a log record describing the change to the WAL on disk. If the system crashes, recovery replays the WAL to reconstruct any changes that didn't make it to data pages. The WAL guarantees that committed transactions survive crashes.
words.longDefinition: Write-Ahead Logging enforces two rules: log before data (the WAL record must reach durable storage before the modified page may be written to disk) and log before commit (all log records for a transaction must be durable before the commit acknowledgment is sent to the client). The WAL is a sequential, append-only file — sequential writes are the fastest durable-write pattern available and avoid the random-write cost of flushing modified data pages. Every WAL record carries a Log Sequence Number (LSN), a monotonically increasing byte offset. Each data page's header stores the LSN of the last modification, so during recovery the engine can compare page LSN to WAL LSN and know exactly which records need to be replayed. PostgreSQL stores WAL in pg_wal/ as 16 MB segment files; InnoDB uses ib_logfile0 and ib_logfile1 as a circular redo log. WAL is also the replication mechanism: standbys receive WAL records from the primary and replay them, staying in sync without any knowledge of the application.
words.connector: Think of WAL like a flight recorder (black box) in an aircraft: every action is logged to a durable sequential record before it takes effect, so after a crash the investigators can reconstruct exactly what happened.
words.techContext: WAL is the reason fsync matters: if the OS buffers WAL writes in a write-back cache and the system crashes before they reach durable storage, the 'logged before commit' guarantee is broken, and committed transactions are silently lost.
words.exampleSentence: After the power failure, PostgreSQL replayed 340 MB of WAL from the last checkpoint and recovered the database to the exact committed state without losing a single transaction.
words.etymology: Write-Ahead Log: 'write-ahead' because log records must be written before ('ahead of') the data pages they describe. The term was formalized in the ARIES paper (Mohan et al., IBM 1992).

words.shortDefinition: Multi-Version Concurrency Control: readers see a consistent snapshot by reading old row versions instead of blocking writers.
words.simpleDefinition: MVCC lets readers and writers run concurrently without blocking each other. Instead of locking a row when it's being updated, the database keeps multiple versions of the row. Readers see the version that was current when their transaction started. Writers create new versions. Nobody waits for anybody else.
words.longDefinition: Multi-Version Concurrency Control solves the readers-block-writers problem by maintaining multiple versions of each row simultaneously. When a transaction updates a row, the old version is preserved rather than overwritten. A reading transaction sees the version that was current at its snapshot timestamp, even if subsequent transactions have since updated or deleted the row. PostgreSQL stores old row versions (dead tuples) directly in the heap alongside live tuples. Each tuple carries two transaction ID fields (xmin/xmax) — the transaction that created it and the transaction that deleted or superseded it. A reader's snapshot determines which xmin/xmax combinations are visible. InnoDB takes a different approach: row updates write new versions to the clustered index but store undo log records in a separate undo tablespace; readers reconstruct old versions by applying undo records backward from the current version. MVCC gives readers a non-blocking consistent snapshot and allows concurrent writes as long as they target different rows. The cost is space amplification (dead tuples accumulate until VACUUM cleans them in PostgreSQL) and read amplification when version chains grow long.
words.connector: Think of MVCC like a library's checkout system where every returned book is kept on a history shelf instead of being replaced — a reader who checked out the 2020 edition can finish reading it even while someone else is updating the 2024 edition.
words.techContext: MVCC is why long-running transactions in PostgreSQL can cause table bloat: dead tuple versions cannot be vacuumed away while any active transaction's snapshot predates them, so the heap grows without bound.
words.exampleSentence: Because PostgreSQL uses MVCC, the reporting query running a full table scan at 3 AM sees a perfectly consistent snapshot of the data without blocking or being blocked by the OLTP writes happening simultaneously.

codeExample.code:
-- PostgreSQL: inspect MVCC visibility fields on heap tuples
SELECT xmin, xmax, ctid, order_id
FROM orders
LIMIT 5;
-- xmin: transaction that INSERTed this version
-- xmax: transaction that DELETEd/UPDATEd it (0 = still live)

-- Dead tuples accumulate until VACUUM
SELECT n_live_tup, n_dead_tup
FROM pg_stat_user_tables
WHERE relname = 'orders';

words.etymology: Multi-Version Concurrency Control was described by Reed (1978) and Bernstein & Goodman (1983). PostgreSQL's MVCC implementation dates to its origins as Postgres (Stonebraker, 1986), which was designed from the start with time-travel queries in mind.

words.shortDefinition: The execution strategy chosen by the optimizer: which indexes to use, join order, join algorithm.
words.simpleDefinition: A query plan is the database's step-by-step recipe for answering a SQL query. The optimizer considers many possible plans (different indexes, join orders, and join algorithms) and picks the one with the lowest estimated cost. The plan is a tree of physical operators — index scans, hash joins, sorts — that the executor runs top-down.
words.longDefinition: After parsing and analyzing a SQL statement, the query optimizer generates a query plan: a tree of physical operators that the executor will run. Each node in the tree is a concrete operation: SeqScan (read all heap pages), IndexScan (traverse a B-tree), IndexOnlyScan (use covering index), HashJoin, MergeJoin, NestedLoop, Sort, Aggregate. The optimizer enumerates candidate plans by considering all usable access paths for each table, all valid join orderings (using dynamic programming for small N, GEQO for large N), and all applicable join algorithms. It estimates the cost of each plan using table statistics (row counts, column histograms, NDV) and picks the minimum-cost plan. A 'bad' plan — caused by stale statistics, a high-cardinality correlated subquery, or an extremely selective predicate — can cause a query to run 100× slower than necessary. EXPLAIN reveals the chosen plan; EXPLAIN ANALYZE runs the plan and shows actual row counts versus estimates, making plan regressions diagnosable.
words.connector: Think of a query plan like GPS navigation: the system evaluates multiple routes (different roads, highways, shortcuts) using traffic estimates and picks the fastest one — except the database is routing through data pages instead of city streets.
words.techContext: When a query suddenly becomes slow after a data load, the first step is EXPLAIN ANALYZE to compare estimated vs actual row counts at each node — a large discrepancy reveals that statistics are stale and ANALYZE is needed.
words.exampleSentence: The query plan switched from a hash join to a nested loop after the statistics were refreshed, reducing execution time from 45 seconds to 800 ms by correctly estimating the small output of the inner relation.

codeExample.code:
-- PostgreSQL: show query plan with cost estimates
EXPLAIN
SELECT o.*, c.name
FROM orders o JOIN customers c ON o.customer_id = c.id
WHERE o.total > 1000;

-- Run the plan and show actual vs estimated rows
EXPLAIN (ANALYZE, BUFFERS)
SELECT o.*, c.name
FROM orders o JOIN customers c ON o.customer_id = c.id
WHERE o.total > 1000;

words.etymology: Plan from Latin planus ('flat, level'), referring to a laid-out scheme of action. Query plan as a term was established in System R's optimizer paper (Selinger et al., 1979), which is the direct ancestor of every modern SQL optimizer.

words.shortDefinition: A SQL command that shows the query plan and estimated costs the optimizer chose for a statement.
words.simpleDefinition: EXPLAIN is the database developer's essential tool for understanding why a query is slow. It displays the plan tree the optimizer chose — which indexes it uses, which join algorithms it picked, and the estimated row counts and costs at each step. EXPLAIN ANALYZE also executes the query and shows actual timings and row counts alongside the estimates.
words.longDefinition: EXPLAIN is a SQL meta-command that returns the optimizer's chosen plan for a statement without (by default) executing it. The output is a plan tree with each node annotated by: the operator type, estimated startup cost, estimated total cost, estimated row count, and estimated average row width. PostgreSQL's EXPLAIN output uses an indented text format; the EXPLAIN (FORMAT JSON) option produces machine-readable output for tooling. EXPLAIN ANALYZE actually executes the query and augments each plan node with actual timing, actual row counts, and loop counts. The critical diagnostic insight is the gap between estimated and actual rows — a large discrepancy (e.g., estimated 2 rows, actual 5 million) indicates stale statistics or a selectivity estimation failure that caused the optimizer to choose the wrong plan. EXPLAIN (ANALYZE, BUFFERS) additionally shows buffer pool hits and misses, revealing whether a slow query is CPU-bound or I/O-bound. Most production query performance investigations start and end with EXPLAIN ANALYZE.
words.connector: Think of EXPLAIN like opening the hood of a car and seeing the engine blueprint — it does not fix the problem, but it tells you exactly which component is doing the work and how efficiently.
words.techContext: Always use EXPLAIN ANALYZE on a replica or staging environment first — the ANALYZE option actually executes the query, which could modify data if the statement is a DML operation without a ROLLBACK wrapper.
words.exampleSentence: EXPLAIN ANALYZE revealed that the join was estimating 3 rows but scanning 2 million, causing the optimizer to pick a nested loop where a hash join would have been 500× faster — running ANALYZE on the table fixed the plan.

codeExample.code:
-- Basic plan (no execution):
EXPLAIN SELECT * FROM orders WHERE customer_id = 42;

-- Full diagnostic: execute + show timing + buffer stats
EXPLAIN (ANALYZE, BUFFERS, FORMAT TEXT)
SELECT o.id, c.email
FROM orders o
JOIN customers c ON o.customer_id = c.id
WHERE o.created_at > NOW() - INTERVAL '7 days';
-- Key fields to examine:
--   rows=N (estimated) vs actual rows=M
--   Buffers: shared hit=X read=Y  (Y>0 means disk I/O)

words.etymology: From Latin explanare ('to make flat, to make plain'); as a SQL command, EXPLAIN has been part of the standard since early relational systems and appears in every major RDBMS with similar syntax.

words.shortDefinition: Postgres background process that removes dead MVCC tuple versions and reclaims disk space.
words.simpleDefinition: Because PostgreSQL's MVCC keeps old row versions in the heap rather than discarding them immediately, dead tuples accumulate over time. VACUUM scans heap pages, identifies tuples that are no longer visible to any active transaction, marks their space as reusable, and updates the free space map. Without regular VACUUM, tables bloat indefinitely and eventually transaction ID wraparound causes database downtime.
words.longDefinition: PostgreSQL's MVCC model stores old row versions (dead tuples) in the heap until they are explicitly reclaimed. A dead tuple is a row version that is no longer visible to any current or future transaction — its xmax is a committed transaction ID that predates all active snapshots. VACUUM identifies and marks these slots as free, allowing new tuples to reuse the space. VACUUM also updates the free space map (FSM) so the engine knows which pages have room for new inserts. Crucially, VACUUM must also advance the visibility map — marking pages that contain only live tuples as 'all-visible' — which enables index-only scans and reduces future vacuum work. Autovacuum, PostgreSQL's background daemon, runs VACUUM and ANALYZE automatically based on configurable thresholds (autovacuum_vacuum_scale_factor). VACUUM FULL is a more aggressive variant that rewrites the entire table into a new heap, reclaiming space at the OS level, but it holds a full exclusive lock on the table for its duration and should be used sparingly. PostgreSQL also requires periodic vacuuming to prevent transaction ID (XID) wraparound: XIDs are 32-bit integers; after 2 billion transactions, the counter wraps and old transactions would appear to be in the future — a catastrophic data visibility failure.
words.connector: Think of VACUUM like a janitor who sweeps up after MVCC's cleanup crew — MVCC keeps old versions around for in-progress readers; VACUUM comes in after everyone has left and throws them away.
words.techContext: Monitor n_dead_tup in pg_stat_user_tables. A ratio of dead to live tuples above 20% on a heavily-written table indicates autovacuum is not keeping up — increase autovacuum_vacuum_scale_factor or trigger manual VACUUM.
words.exampleSentence: After the bulk DELETE removed 40 million rows, we ran VACUUM ANALYZE immediately to reclaim the dead tuple space and refresh statistics before the next batch of queries hit the now-sparse table.
words.etymology: From Latin vacuum ('empty space'); used in PostgreSQL to describe the process of clearing empty (dead) tuple slots, coined in the original PostgreSQL codebase in the early 1990s.

words.shortDefinition: When a B+ tree leaf fills up, it splits into two pages and promotes a separator key to the parent.
words.simpleDefinition: When an insert arrives at a full B+ tree leaf page, the engine cannot fit the new key. It must split the page: allocate a new sibling, move the upper half of keys to it, and insert a separator key into the parent pointing to the new sibling. If the parent is also full, the split cascades upward — potentially all the way to creating a new root.
words.longDefinition: A page split is the most structurally complex write operation in a B+ tree. The sequence for a leaf split: detect overflow (free space < new record size); allocate a new right sibling page from the free page list; redistribute keys — typically the upper half move to the new sibling; update the leaf-level linked list (old page's next-pointer → new sibling; sibling's next-pointer → old page's former successor); promote the smallest key of the new right sibling as a separator key into the parent internal node. If the parent also overflows, the split repeats for the parent — but for internal nodes, the median key is pushed up (removed) rather than copied. The only way a B-tree grows taller is when the root splits: a new root is allocated containing just the promoted key and two child pointers. In a WAL-based engine, all modified pages are logged before they are written, so a crash mid-split is safe: recovery replays the full split. Frequent page splits indicate under-provisioned fill factor or a random-key insert pattern. A fill factor below 100% leaves headroom so that future inserts can land in-place without triggering a split.
words.connector: Think of a page split like a filing cabinet drawer that gets too full — you pull out half the folders, put them in a new drawer, then update the cabinet's label system to point to the right drawer for each range.
words.techContext: Random UUID v4 primary keys cause constant mid-tree page splits in InnoDB because inserts scatter across all leaf pages. Sequential keys (AUTO_INCREMENT, ULID) hit only the right-most leaf and trigger only right-edge splits, which are much cheaper.
words.exampleSentence: The INSERT workload on the UUID-keyed table was hitting 30 page splits per second, generating write amplification that doubled I/O — switching to sequential IDs eliminated all mid-tree splits.

codeExample.code:
-- PostgreSQL: monitor index fragmentation (bloat from splits)
SELECT
  bt_page_stats.live_items,
  bt_page_stats.dead_items,
  bt_page_stats.avg_item_size,
  bt_page_stats.free_size
FROM bt_page_stats('idx_orders_user_id', 1);

-- REINDEX reclaims split-induced fragmentation:
REINDEX INDEX CONCURRENTLY idx_orders_user_id;

words.etymology: Page from database engineering (the fixed-size I/O unit); split from Old English splittan ('to divide'). The page split algorithm was described in Knuth's The Art of Computer Programming Vol. 3 (1973).

words.shortDefinition: A single row as physically stored on a page, including header bits for MVCC visibility.
words.simpleDefinition: A tuple is the physical representation of a row on a database page. It includes the actual column data plus a tuple header containing MVCC visibility fields (xmin, xmax in PostgreSQL) and flags. Unlike the logical concept of a 'row', a tuple is tied to a specific physical location — a particular slot on a particular page.
words.longDefinition: In relational database theory, a tuple is a member of a relation (table) — an ordered sequence of typed values. In PostgreSQL's physical storage, a tuple is the on-disk byte representation of a row, including: a tuple header (23 bytes in PostgreSQL) carrying xmin (transaction ID that created this version), xmax (transaction ID that deleted/updated it, or 0 if live), infomask bits (null bitmap, HOT flags, lock info), and ctid (current physical address for HOT chains). The header is followed by an optional null bitmap and then the actual column data. Because PostgreSQL's MVCC stores multiple versions of a row as separate tuples in the heap, a single logical row may correspond to several tuples — the live version plus accumulated dead versions awaiting VACUUM. Tuple size directly affects page capacity and therefore B-tree fan-out: wide tuples mean fewer per page, deeper trees, and more I/O. PostgreSQL uses TOAST (The Oversized-Attribute Storage Technique) to handle tuples that exceed roughly 2 KB, storing large values out-of-line in a separate TOAST table with a pointer in the main page.
words.connector: Think of a tuple like a physical index card in a card catalog: the card has a header with catalog metadata (visibility, transaction IDs) and the actual content on the rest of the card — but a single book might have multiple cards if the catalog entry was revised.
words.techContext: When diagnosing table bloat, think in tuples: each UPDATE in PostgreSQL creates a new tuple and marks the old one dead. A column updated 100 times generates 100 dead tuples per row, all occupying heap space until vacuumed.
words.exampleSentence: VACUUM cleared 18 million dead tuples from the events table — each status-column update had left a dead version behind, bloating the heap to 6× the logical data size.

codeExample.code:
-- PostgreSQL: inspect raw tuple fields on a heap page
SELECT t_xmin, t_xmax, t_ctid,
       t_infomask::bit(16) AS flags
FROM heap_page_items(get_raw_page('orders', 0))
LIMIT 10;
-- t_xmax = 0 → live tuple
-- t_xmax = committed XID → dead tuple, pending VACUUM

words.etymology: Tuple from Latin tuplus ('fold, layer'), as in double, triple, quadruple. In database theory, formalised by Codd (1970); in PostgreSQL's source code, the term HeapTuple refers to the physical on-disk row representation.

words.shortDefinition: A page format with a slot directory at one end and variable-length tuples packed from the other end.
words.simpleDefinition: A slotted page is the standard page layout for storing variable-length rows. A slot directory grows inward from the top of the page; tuples pack inward from the bottom. The gap between them is free space. External pointers reference rows by (page, slot) rather than byte offset, so tuples can be compacted within the page without breaking any references.
words.longDefinition: The slotted page format solves three related problems: storing variable-length records, reclaiming space after deletes, and allowing tuples to move within a page for compaction — all without invalidating external references. The layout has a page header at the top, followed by a slot directory growing downward. Each slot entry is small (4 bytes in PostgreSQL: a 15-bit offset, 2-bit flags, 15-bit length). Tuples are packed from the bottom upward. Free space sits between the bottom of the slot directory (pd_lower) and the top of the tuple area (pd_upper). When a tuple is deleted, its slot is flagged DEAD but not removed — the slot index is stable. When a new tuple is inserted, its data goes at pd_upper, and a new slot entry is added at pd_lower. VACUUM compacts a page by sliding live tuples together, updating only the slot offsets — external CTIDs (page + slot) remain valid. This indirection is what makes stable row addressing possible in the presence of in-page compaction. PostgreSQL's heap pages and B-tree pages both use this format; InnoDB uses a similar structure called a compact row format.
words.connector: Think of a slotted page like a parking garage where each parking spot has a fixed number on the wall (the slot) but cars can be repositioned within the garage — the spot number never changes, even if the car moves to a different physical location.
words.techContext: The slotted page design is why ctid (page, slot) is a stable address in PostgreSQL: VACUUM can compact tuples within a page and update slot offsets, but the (page, slot) tuple identifier that secondary indexes hold remains valid.
words.exampleSentence: After understanding the slotted page layout, the engineer realized that VACUUM's compaction step moves tuples within pages without invalidating any index entries, because indexes hold (page, slot) CTIDs, not byte offsets.

codeExample.code:
-- PostgreSQL: inspect slotted page internals
SELECT * FROM page_header(get_raw_page('orders', 0));
-- pd_lower: end of slot directory
-- pd_upper: start of tuple area
-- Free space = pd_upper - pd_lower

-- Inspect individual slot entries
SELECT lp, lp_off, lp_flags, lp_len
FROM heap_page_items(get_raw_page('orders', 0));

words.etymology: Slot from Middle English slot ('a narrow opening'); slotted page as a term was popularized by Ramakrishnan and Gehrke's Database Management Systems textbook and is standard in CMU's 15-445 course materials.

words.shortDefinition: Table-level metadata (row counts, column histograms) collected by ANALYZE and used by the optimizer.
words.simpleDefinition: Statistics are the optimizer's information about what the data in a table looks like: how many rows exist, how many distinct values a column has, the distribution of values (histograms), and correlations between columns and physical row order. Without accurate statistics, the optimizer picks wrong plans. ANALYZE collects fresh statistics; autovacuum runs it automatically.
words.longDefinition: The PostgreSQL query optimizer is a cost-based optimizer: it estimates the cost of each candidate plan using a statistical model of the data. Statistics are the inputs to that model. PostgreSQL's pg_statistic catalog stores per-column statistics: n_distinct (number of distinct values, or a fraction of total rows if negative), most_common_vals and most_common_freqs (a sampled list of the most frequent values and their frequencies), histogram_bounds (quantile boundaries for non-common values), and correlation (Pearson correlation between column sort order and physical heap order — 1.0 means perfectly correlated, 0 means random). ANALYZE samples up to default_statistics_target × 300 rows (default: 100 × 300 = 30 000) per table per column. Stale statistics — especially after a bulk load that adds millions of rows — cause the optimizer to dramatically misestimate row counts, leading to wrong join algorithms and index choices. The symptoms: a query that runs fine on staging but is slow on production after a data import, or a plan that uses nested loop on a relation the optimizer believes has 100 rows but actually has 10 million.
words.connector: Think of statistics like weather forecast models: the forecast quality depends entirely on how current and accurate the underlying sensor data is — stale data gives wrong predictions, no matter how sophisticated the model.
words.techContext: After any bulk load of more than 10% of a table's rows, run ANALYZE manually. Autovacuum's threshold is proportional to table size, so on very large tables it may not trigger quickly enough after a big import.
words.exampleSentence: The deployment ran fine in staging (100 K rows) but triggered full table scans in production (50 M rows) because ANALYZE had not been run after the migration, leaving the optimizer thinking the production table was small.
words.etymology: From German Statistik, from Modern Latin statisticum ('of the state'); in database context, formalised as 'column statistics' in the System R optimizer paper (Selinger et al., 1979), which introduced histogram-based cardinality estimation.

words.shortDefinition: An index that includes all columns a query needs, so the heap table never needs to be read.
words.simpleDefinition: A covering index satisfies a query entirely from the index itself — the index leaf pages contain every column the query projects and filters on, so the engine never needs to fetch the underlying heap row. This eliminates the heap fetch, turning a two-I/O operation (index leaf + heap page) into a one-I/O index-only scan.
words.longDefinition: A covering index is any index whose leaf entries contain all columns referenced by a specific query, including columns in SELECT, WHERE, JOIN ON, and ORDER BY clauses. When the optimizer recognizes a covering index opportunity, it produces an IndexOnlyScan plan node (PostgreSQL) or a 'Using index' plan (MySQL). This eliminates the heap fetch entirely: the executor reads index leaf pages, projects the requested columns, and returns results. The performance gain can be dramatic for narrow projections on wide tables. In PostgreSQL, covering indexes are created using the INCLUDE clause: CREATE INDEX idx ON orders(customer_id) INCLUDE (total, status). The INCLUDE columns are stored in the leaf pages but not in the internal routing nodes — they are available for projection but cannot be used as range predicates. InnoDB automatically covers secondary index lookups when all needed columns are either the index key or the primary key (which every InnoDB secondary index carries implicitly). The tradeoff: covering indexes are wider (more data per leaf page), increasing write amplification on every INSERT/UPDATE that touches a covered column.
words.connector: Think of a covering index like a summary table at a trade show — it has all the information a visitor needs right there without requiring them to travel to the actual exhibit booth (the heap).
words.techContext: When EXPLAIN shows 'Heap Fetches: N' under an IndexOnlyScan, the visibility map has not marked those pages as all-visible — run VACUUM to update it and eliminate the remaining heap fetches.
words.exampleSentence: Adding INCLUDE (total, status) to the customer_id index turned the most expensive reporting query from an index scan plus 200 000 heap fetches into a pure index-only scan, cutting execution time from 3.4 s to 180 ms.

codeExample.code:
-- PostgreSQL: covering index with INCLUDE clause
CREATE INDEX idx_orders_customer_covering
  ON orders (customer_id)
  INCLUDE (order_date, total, status);

-- This query can now use an index-only scan:
SELECT order_date, total, status
FROM orders
WHERE customer_id = 42
ORDER BY order_date;
-- EXPLAIN shows: Index Only Scan, Heap Fetches: 0 (after VACUUM)

words.etymology: Covering in the sense of 'covering all requirements'; the term covering index was popularized in Lahdenmäki & Leach's Relational Database Index Design and the Optimizers (2005) and is now used across all major RDBMS documentation.

words.shortDefinition: An index with a WHERE clause that only indexes a subset of rows, saving space and write cost.
words.simpleDefinition: A partial index indexes only the rows that satisfy a predicate, ignoring the rest. If 95% of your orders have status = 'completed' and queries only ever filter on pending orders, a partial index on pending orders is 20× smaller than a full index and has 20× lower write overhead.
words.longDefinition: A partial index is a B-tree (or other access method) built over only the subset of rows that satisfy a WHERE clause specified at index creation time. The WHERE clause is evaluated once during INSERT/UPDATE: rows that satisfy it are indexed; rows that do not are ignored. Partial indexes are valuable when a column has high cardinality for one value category (e.g., 99% of rows have deleted = false) and queries consistently filter on the rare category (deleted = true) or on the common category with an additional selective predicate. Benefits: the index is smaller (fewer leaf pages, fewer levels), write amplification is lower (only 1% of inserts touch the partial index in the deleted = false example), and sequential scans of the index are faster. PostgreSQL supports partial indexes natively. InnoDB does not support partial indexes directly, but functional indexes and prefix indexes provide related functionality. The optimizer will use a partial index only when the query's WHERE clause is implied by the index predicate — the optimizer must be able to prove the query cannot return rows the partial index does not cover.
words.connector: Think of a partial index like a VIP guest list at a venue — instead of listing every person who might ever attend, you only track the select subset you care about, making the list shorter and faster to search.
words.techContext: A classic use case: partial index on active sessions (WHERE expires_at > NOW()) — only live sessions are indexed, dramatically shrinking the index on a table that accumulates millions of expired sessions.
words.exampleSentence: A partial index on WHERE status = 'pending' reduced index size from 2 GB to 40 MB and cut the 'find all pending orders' query time from 800 ms to 3 ms on a table of 50 million rows.

codeExample.code:
-- PostgreSQL: partial index on the rare/active subset
CREATE INDEX idx_orders_pending
  ON orders (created_at)
  WHERE status = 'pending';

-- This query will use the partial index:
SELECT * FROM orders
WHERE status = 'pending'
  AND created_at > NOW() - INTERVAL '24 hours';

-- Enforce uniqueness only on active rows:
CREATE UNIQUE INDEX idx_users_active_email
  ON users (email)
  WHERE is_deleted = false;

words.etymology: Partial from Latin partialis ('of a part'); the concept of partial indexes was introduced in Stonebraker's 1989 paper 'The Case for Partial Indexes' and implemented in PostgreSQL in the same era.

words.shortDefinition: The percentage of each B-tree page filled at creation; free space absorbs future inserts without splits.
words.simpleDefinition: Fill factor controls how tightly the engine packs data into B-tree pages when the index is built or a page is written for the first time. A fill factor of 70% leaves 30% of each page free. Future inserts into that page's key range can land in-place without triggering a split — trading wasted space now for avoided write amplification later.
words.longDefinition: When a B+ tree page is written, the engine does not have to fill it completely. The fill factor percentage determines how full each page will be at creation or during bulk load. A fill factor of 100% packs every page tightly; future inserts into middle pages immediately require a split. A fill factor of 70% leaves 30% headroom; inserts into that key range can land in-place. The tradeoff: lower fill factor means more pages for the same data (higher space amplification, lower fan-out, more I/O for range scans), but fewer splits and less write amplification for random-insert workloads. PostgreSQL allows per-index fill factor via CREATE INDEX ... WITH (fillfactor=70). For heap tables, a lower fill factor on the table itself benefits Heap-Only Tuple (HOT) updates: if the updated row's new version fits on the same page as the old version, PostgreSQL can update without touching any secondary indexes. InnoDB uses a fixed default of approximately 93% for clustered indexes. Fill factor tuning is most impactful on tables with heavy random-key inserts (UUID primary keys) or heavily updated columns where HOT updates are valuable.
words.connector: Think of fill factor like packing a moving box: packing it 70% full now leaves room for a few more items you discover later, avoiding having to open a new box and reorganize — at the cost of using more boxes overall.
words.techContext: For a table with heavy UPDATE workloads in PostgreSQL, set heap fill factor to 70–80% to enable HOT updates. For index-only-scan-heavy workloads, keep fill factor at 90–100% to minimize index size.
words.exampleSentence: Reducing the fill factor on the email index from 100% to 75% eliminated the nightly split storm on the registration table, at the cost of a 30% larger index that still fit comfortably in the buffer pool.

codeExample.code:
-- PostgreSQL: create index with custom fill factor
CREATE INDEX idx_orders_customer
  ON orders (customer_id)
  WITH (fillfactor = 75);

-- Set fill factor on the heap table (for HOT updates)
ALTER TABLE orders SET (fillfactor = 80);

-- Rebuild to apply the new fill factor:
VACUUM FULL orders;  -- or CLUSTER / REINDEX

words.etymology: Fill factor is a manufacturing and engineering term for the ratio of material to total capacity; adopted into B-tree literature in Knuth's The Art of Computer Programming Vol. 3 (1973) and standard in database tuning guides since.

words.shortDefinition: The ratio of bytes written to disk versus bytes logically written by the application.
words.simpleDefinition: Write amplification measures how much extra I/O a database generates per logical write. A WAL-based system writes each change at least twice: once to the sequential log and once to the data page. B-tree page splits, secondary index updates, and MVCC tuple versions all add more. High write amplification shortens SSD lifespan and limits sustained write throughput.
words.longDefinition: Write amplification (WA) is the ratio: physical bytes written to storage / logical bytes written by the application. It stacks multiplicatively across layers. At the WAL layer: every write generates a log record plus eventually a data page write — baseline WA ≈ 2×. At the B-tree layer: updating a 50-byte row requires writing an entire 16 KB page — WA ≈ 327× for that write (mitigated by batching many rows per page flush). Secondary indexes multiply this further: a table with 5 secondary indexes on updated columns rewrites 6 B-tree leaf pages per update (primary + 5 secondaries). At the SSD level: NAND flash cannot overwrite in place; the firmware's flash translation layer (FTL) must erase entire blocks (512 KB–4 MB) before writing, introducing its own WA. Database WA, compaction WA (in LSM engines), and FTL WA multiply together. For LSM engines using leveled compaction, Petrov (Database Internals, 2019) measures typical WA at 10–30×. The RUM conjecture formalizes the trade-off: no access method can simultaneously minimize read, write, and space amplification. B-trees optimize for low read and space amplification at the cost of moderate write amplification; LSM-trees trade write amplification for better write throughput.
words.connector: Think of write amplification like printing a one-page document: you write 500 words, the printer uses a full toner cartridge to lay down ink on the entire page surface — far more material consumed than the logical content requires.
words.techContext: Monitor write amplification using iostat (bytes written by the OS) vs application-level write metrics. On an InnoDB server, unexpected WA spikes often trace to secondary index maintenance on a heavily-updated column — consider partial indexes or deferred indexing.
words.exampleSentence: After instrumenting our write path, we discovered 28× write amplification: each 100-byte event write generated 2.8 KB of actual disk I/O across WAL, heap page, and four secondary index updates.
words.etymology: Amplification from Latin amplificare ('to enlarge'); write amplification as a term was popularized in SSD and flash storage literature around 2008 and adopted into database internals discourse by Petrov's Database Internals (O'Reilly, 2019).

words.shortDefinition: The ratio of bytes read from disk versus bytes of user data returned by a query.
words.simpleDefinition: Read amplification measures how much extra data the database reads to answer a query. A B-tree traversal reads 3–4 pages to deliver one leaf page. A row-store SELECT of 3 out of 100 columns loads all 100. A secondary index lookup reads the index leaf and then the heap page. All of these inflate the bytes read relative to the bytes the query actually needs.
words.longDefinition: Read amplification (RA) is the ratio: physical bytes read from storage / bytes of user data returned by the query. Major sources: B-tree traversal overhead (reading 3–5 internal pages to reach one leaf page; for a small row on an 8 KB page the RA from tree traversal alone can be 100–500×, though upper levels stay hot in the buffer pool and rarely touch disk), MVCC version chain traversal (following multiple dead tuple versions to find the visible one), row-store column amplification (a SELECT of 3 out of 100 columns still loads the full page containing all 100 columns), and LSM-tree multi-level probing (without Bloom filters, a point lookup must check the memtable and each SSTable level). The RUM conjecture positions read amplification in tension with write amplification and space amplification: B-trees minimize RA at the cost of moderate write amplification; LSM size-tiered compaction minimizes write amplification at the cost of higher RA. Covering indexes, column stores, and Bloom filters all exist to reduce RA. The buffer pool masks RA when the working set fits in RAM — the amplification only becomes visible when cold data must be fetched from disk.
words.connector: Think of read amplification like a librarian who must read the entire encyclopedia volume to find one paragraph — the entire volume comes off the shelf (page I/O), even though you only needed 200 words.
words.techContext: High read amplification is often invisible behind a warm buffer pool. To detect it, measure I/O at the storage layer (iostat bytes_read) vs actual data returned. A gap indicates RA — fix it with covering indexes, statistics refresh, or tighter query predicates.
words.exampleSentence: The OLAP query scanned a 200-column row-store table to aggregate three columns, producing 66× read amplification — moving those columns to a covering index reduced I/O by 60× and cut query time from 90 s to 1.4 s.
words.etymology: Amplification from Latin amplificare ('to enlarge'); read amplification as a paired term to write amplification appears in the RUM conjecture paper (Athanassoulis et al., CIDR 2016) and Petrov's Database Internals.

words.shortDefinition: The ratio of bytes used on disk versus bytes of live logical data (overhead from indexes, MVCC, fragmentation).
words.simpleDefinition: Space amplification measures how many bytes of storage the database consumes per byte of live logical data. Secondary indexes duplicate columns. Dead MVCC tuples accumulate until vacuumed. B-tree page fragmentation leaves holes after deletes. LSM tiers keep multiple copies pre-compaction. Together they can push storage cost to 5–10× the raw data size.
words.longDefinition: Space amplification (SA) is the ratio: bytes consumed on durable storage / bytes of live logical data. Sources: indexes (each secondary index duplicates the indexed columns plus a primary key pointer — a table with 10 wide secondary indexes can easily use 3–5× its raw data size in index pages); MVCC dead tuples (PostgreSQL's heap accumulates old row versions; a heavily-updated table with infrequent VACUUM can reach 10× logical data size); B-tree page fragmentation (after many random inserts and deletes, pages accumulate holes; a heavily fragmented B-tree can have 50% or more of its pages half-empty); LSM pre-compaction overhead (size-tiered compaction allows 2–3× SA before compaction fires; leveled compaction holds SA closer to 1.1×). SA does not affect latency directly — it is primarily a storage cost and an indirect I/O concern (more pages to scan for sequential reads). The RUM conjecture frames SA as the third vertex: reducing SA (e.g., leveled LSM compaction) increases write amplification. Monitoring pg_stat_user_tables.n_dead_tup and comparing pg_total_relation_size to pg_relation_size reveals SA for PostgreSQL tables.
words.connector: Think of space amplification like the overhead in a filing cabinet: indexes are extra copies of the filing labels, MVCC dead tuples are old superseded versions you haven't shredded yet, and fragmentation is the half-empty folders scattered through the drawers.
words.techContext: Space amplification compounds silently. A table with n_dead_tup / n_live_tup > 2 needs immediate VACUUM. Use pg_repack for tables where VACUUM FULL's exclusive lock is unacceptable but fragmentation has grown extreme.
words.exampleSentence: The billing table's pg_total_relation_size showed 48 GB while logical row data was only 6 GB — 8× space amplification from 12 secondary indexes and three years of dead tuples from missed autovacuum jobs.
words.etymology: Amplification from Latin amplificare; space amplification as a term appears alongside read and write amplification in the RUM conjecture paper (Athanassoulis et al., CIDR 2016) as the third vertex of the storage trade-off triangle.

words.shortDefinition: The database component that grants, queues, and detects conflicts for row, page, and table locks.
words.simpleDefinition: The lock manager is the concurrency traffic cop inside the database. It maintains a lock table mapping every locked resource (row, page, table) to the transactions holding or waiting for locks. Before any transaction can access a shared resource, it must ask the lock manager. The lock manager detects deadlocks and aborts one victim transaction to break them.
words.longDefinition: The lock manager enforces isolation by controlling which transactions can concurrently access which resources. It maintains a lock table: a hash map from resource identifiers (row TIDs, page IDs, relation OIDs) to lock mode and holder/waiter lists. PostgreSQL supports multiple lock modes with a compatibility matrix: ACCESS SHARE (held by SELECT), ROW SHARE (SELECT FOR UPDATE), ROW EXCLUSIVE (INSERT/UPDATE/DELETE), SHARE UPDATE EXCLUSIVE (VACUUM), SHARE (CREATE INDEX), and ACCESS EXCLUSIVE (DROP TABLE, LOCK TABLE). When a transaction requests a lock and finds a conflicting holder, it is queued as a waiter. A deadlock occurs when a cycle exists in the waiter graph: T1 holds lock A, wants B; T2 holds B, wants A. PostgreSQL's lock manager runs deadlock detection periodically (deadlock_timeout default 1 s) and aborts one victim to break the cycle. InnoDB uses row-level locks with gap locks and next-key locks to prevent phantom reads under REPEATABLE READ isolation without predicate locks. The lock manager interacts with MVCC: PostgreSQL uses MVCC for read isolation (readers never wait for writers) and row-level locks only for write-write conflicts.
words.connector: Think of the lock manager like an air traffic controller: every plane (transaction) must get clearance before landing on a runway (resource), the controller queues conflicting arrivals, and if two planes are circling waiting for each other, the controller must divert one.
words.techContext: When a query hangs, pg_locks shows all held and waited locks. A long lock chain often reveals a forgotten long-running transaction or an uncommitted migration — always commit DDL operations promptly.
words.exampleSentence: The deployment script held an ACCESS EXCLUSIVE lock on the users table for 8 minutes during an index rebuild, queuing 400 application connections that were each waiting for a simple SELECT.

codeExample.code:
-- PostgreSQL: see all current locks and blocking queries
SELECT
  pg_locks.pid,
  pg_locks.mode,
  pg_locks.granted,
  pg_stat_activity.query
FROM pg_locks
JOIN pg_stat_activity USING (pid)
WHERE NOT pg_locks.granted
ORDER BY pg_locks.pid;

words.etymology: Lock from Old English loc ('fastening'); manager from Latin manuarius ('of the hand'). Lock management as a database concept was formalised in Gray's 'Notes on Data Base Operating Systems' (IBM, 1978).

words.shortDefinition: A buffer pool page that has been modified but not yet flushed to disk.
words.simpleDefinition: A dirty page is a page in the buffer pool whose in-memory content differs from what is stored on disk — it has been modified (written) but not yet flushed. Dirty pages must be written to disk before they can be evicted. They also interact with WAL: a dirty page cannot be written to disk unless the corresponding WAL records have already been flushed.
words.longDefinition: When a transaction modifies a row, the engine changes the row's page in the buffer pool and marks that frame as dirty (dirty bit = 1). The page now contains data that is not on disk. Dirty pages are subject to three constraints. First, WAL ordering: a dirty page cannot be written to disk (flushed) before the WAL records that describe its changes are flushed — this is the write-ahead guarantee. Second, checkpoint interaction: the checkpointer periodically flushes dirty pages to reduce the amount of WAL that must be replayed on crash recovery. After a checkpoint, dirty pages from before the checkpoint have been flushed; only pages dirtied after the checkpoint need recovery. Third, eviction: when the buffer pool runs out of clean frames and the replacement policy selects a dirty victim, the engine must write it to disk before loading a new page — this is an eviction I/O. The dirty page table (DPT), used in the ARIES recovery algorithm, is an in-memory structure tracking each dirty page's recLSN: the earliest WAL LSN that modified this page, which is the earliest log record needed to reconstruct the page's current state during crash recovery.
words.connector: Think of a dirty page like a whiteboard someone has written on but not photographed yet — the whiteboard content (buffer pool) is more up-to-date than the last photograph (disk), and you must photograph it before erasing it.
words.techContext: A high ratio of dirty pages in the buffer pool combined with a stall in bgwriter activity can cause checkpoint spikes — the checkpointer must flush a large backlog of dirty pages at once, causing I/O storms. Tune bgwriter_lru_maxpages and checkpoint_completion_target.
words.exampleSentence: The I/O storm at 2 AM was caused by 60% of the buffer pool being dirty pages all flushing during a checkpoint — smoothing dirty page writes across the checkpoint interval via checkpoint_completion_target = 0.9 eliminated the spike.

codeExample.code:
-- PostgreSQL: monitor dirty pages and checkpoint activity
SELECT
  checkpoints_timed,
  checkpoints_req,
  buffers_checkpoint,   -- pages written at checkpoint
  buffers_clean,        -- pages written by bgwriter
  buffers_backend,      -- pages written by backends (bad!)
  buffers_alloc
FROM pg_stat_bgwriter;

words.etymology: Dirty in the computing sense of 'modified and not yet persisted' (a dirty register, a dirty cache line, a dirty buffer); the term appears in early OS and database literature as a standard descriptor for modified-but-unflushed state.

words.shortDefinition: A periodic record in the WAL capturing which pages are dirty and which transactions are active, bounding recovery time.
words.simpleDefinition: A checkpoint is a point in the WAL at which the database guarantees that all dirty pages dirtied before that point have been flushed to disk. After a checkpoint, crash recovery only needs to replay WAL records written after the checkpoint — bounding recovery time regardless of how long the database has been running.
words.longDefinition: Without checkpoints, crash recovery would need to replay the entire WAL from the beginning of time — growing unboundedly. A checkpoint writes a checkpoint record to the WAL and ensures all dirty pages modified before that WAL position are flushed to disk. After the checkpoint, the engine knows: any page whose LSN is older than the checkpoint LSN is already on disk and does not need to be replayed. Recovery starts from the most recent checkpoint rather than from the WAL's beginning, bounding recovery time to the amount of WAL generated since the last checkpoint. PostgreSQL triggers checkpoints at a WAL-size threshold (max_wal_size, default 1 GB) or at a time interval (checkpoint_timeout, default 5 minutes). A fuzzy checkpoint (PostgreSQL's default) allows transactions to continue running while dirty pages flush in the background — avoiding the stall of a sharp checkpoint that halts all writes. ARIES generalizes checkpoints via the transaction table (which transactions are active) and dirty page table (which pages are dirty and their recLSN) — sufficient information to determine exactly where to start the redo phase during recovery.
words.connector: Think of a checkpoint like saving your progress in a video game — you can die and restart from the save point rather than replaying from the beginning, and the game only needs to remember what happened after the save.
words.techContext: Frequent checkpoints (short checkpoint_timeout or small max_wal_size) reduce crash recovery time but increase I/O from more frequent dirty-page flushes. Infrequent checkpoints reduce steady-state I/O but extend recovery time after a crash.
words.exampleSentence: After the server crashed mid-transaction, PostgreSQL replayed only 800 MB of WAL from the last checkpoint rather than the full 50 GB log history, completing crash recovery in 90 seconds.

codeExample.code:
-- PostgreSQL: trigger a manual checkpoint
CHECKPOINT;

-- View checkpoint statistics
SELECT
  checkpoint_lsn,
  prior_checkpoint_lsn,
  pg_wal_lsn_diff(checkpoint_lsn, prior_checkpoint_lsn)
    AS wal_since_prior_checkpoint_bytes
FROM pg_control_checkpoint();

words.etymology: Checkpoint from military and transport usage (a point at which progress is verified); in database context, introduced formally in Gray's transaction processing papers (1978) and central to the ARIES recovery algorithm (Mohan et al., 1992).

words.shortDefinition: The fraction of table rows that satisfy an index predicate; the closer to zero, the more useful the index, and the more likely the planner chooses it over a sequential scan.
words.simpleDefinition: Index selectivity measures how many rows match a given predicate relative to the total rows in a table. High selectivity (close to 0) means very few rows match — the index is highly discriminating and the planner will almost certainly use it. Low selectivity (close to 1) means most rows match — the index narrows almost nothing and the planner typically does a sequential scan instead, because touching every index page plus every heap page is slower than one sequential sweep.
words.longDefinition: The query planner's job is to find the cheapest execution plan. For any predicate that has an index, the planner computes the expected cost of using the index versus scanning the table sequentially. The pivotal input is the estimated fraction of rows that match the predicate, derived from column statistics maintained by ANALYZE (in PostgreSQL: pg_statistic / pg_stats). Index selectivity = (estimated matching rows) / (total rows). A predicate with selectivity 0.001 matches 0.1% of rows — excellent; using the index skips 99.9% of the table. A predicate with selectivity 0.5 matches half the rows — an index scan must fetch half the heap pages in random order, which at typical row sizes is slower than one sequential pass. PostgreSQL's planner has a hard-coded threshold near 5–20% (depending on page cost, random_page_cost setting, and correlation) beyond which it prefers a sequential scan. The threshold shifts when rows are physically ordered close to index order (high correlation in pg_stats.correlation): with correlation ≈ 1.0, index scans remain efficient up to ~50% selectivity because heap pages are accessed nearly sequentially. Key column statistics stored by ANALYZE that affect selectivity estimates: n_distinct (number of distinct values, used for equality predicates), histogram_bounds (value distribution for range predicates), correlation (physical-to-logical ordering), and most_common_vals / most_common_freqs (for skewed distributions like status columns with values 'active'=99%, 'deleted'=1%). When estimates are wrong — due to correlation not captured in statistics, function-wrapped columns (WHERE UPPER(email) = 'X' bypasses the index), or out-of-date statistics — the planner chooses the wrong plan. The fix: run ANALYZE, increase statistics target (ALTER TABLE ... ALTER COLUMN ... SET STATISTICS 500), or add an expression index on UPPER(email).
words.connector: Think of index selectivity like a sieve: a fine-mesh sieve (high selectivity, few holes that match) is worth using because it keeps almost everything back and lets very little through. A coarse sieve (low selectivity) passes most material anyway, so you may as well tip the whole bucket without the extra step.
words.techContext: Setting statistics target to 500 on a skewed status column gave the planner enough histogram detail to correctly estimate that a WHERE status = 'pending' predicate would match 0.3% of rows rather than the default-assumed 20%, switching the plan from a sequential scan to an index scan and halving query time.
words.exampleSentence: The planner chose a sequential scan despite the existing index because the WHERE country = 'US' predicate had 60% selectivity — picking 60% of rows in random order was more expensive than one linear sweep — so the team added a partial index instead.

codeExample.code:
-- PostgreSQL: inspect column selectivity statistics
SELECT
  attname,
  n_distinct,
  correlation,
  most_common_vals,
  most_common_freqs
FROM pg_stats
WHERE tablename = 'orders' AND attname = 'status';

-- Check estimated vs actual row counts in a query plan
EXPLAIN (ANALYZE, BUFFERS)
SELECT * FROM orders WHERE status = 'pending';
-- Rows=… (estimate) vs actual rows=…
-- Large gap → stale/insufficient statistics

-- Raise statistics target for a skewed column
ALTER TABLE orders
  ALTER COLUMN status SET STATISTICS 500;
ANALYZE orders (status);

words.etymology: Selectivity from Latin selectus ('chosen, picked out') — the degree to which a predicate selects (picks out) a subset of rows. The concept is foundational to relational query optimization, formalized in Selinger et al., 'Access Path Selection in a Relational Database Management System' (SIGMOD 1979), the paper that introduced cost-based optimization to SQL databases.

words.shortDefinition: An index using bit arrays per distinct value; excellent for low-cardinality columns in OLAP queries.
words.simpleDefinition: A bitmap index stores one bit array per distinct value of a column. For a 'status' column with values {active, inactive, deleted}, there are three bitmaps — one per value — each with one bit per row. To find all 'active' rows, the engine reads the active bitmap and finds the set bits.
