Multiple bitmaps can be AND/OR-ed together in a single CPU operation, making multi-condition OLAP queries extremely fast.
words.longDefinition: A bitmap index represents each distinct column value as a vector of bits, one bit per row in the table. Bit i is 1 if row i has this value, 0 otherwise. For a column with cardinality C and N rows, the bitmap index uses N × C bits total. The killer feature is bitwise Boolean operations: an AND query on two bitmap indexes is a single bitwise AND on two bit arrays — a SIMD-friendly operation that modern CPUs execute at tens of billions of bits per second. Oracle Database pioneered bitmap indexes for OLAP; PostgreSQL does not support bitmap indexes as a persistent access method, but its query executor uses a dynamic bitmap internally (Bitmap Index Scan → Bitmap Heap Scan) to combine multiple B-tree indexes. Columnar stores like Vertica, Redshift, and DuckDB use compressed bitmap encoding (run-length encoded bitmaps, roaring bitmaps) as a native storage mechanism. Bitmap indexes are ideal for low-cardinality columns (status, region, product_category) in OLAP workloads. They are poor for high-cardinality columns (user_id, email) because the bitmaps become sparse and the compression advantage disappears. They are also poor for write-heavy OLTP because every INSERT/UPDATE requires updating every value's bitmap.
words.connector: Think of a bitmap index like a seating chart with colored dots: one color per seat type (window/aisle/middle) — to find all window seats you scan just the window-seat bitmap row by row rather than reading every seat's full record.
words.techContext: PostgreSQL's Bitmap Index Scan uses the same principle dynamically: the planner scans an index to build an in-memory row-ID bitmap, then accesses heap pages in physical order to avoid random I/O — a hybrid approach combining B-tree precision with sequential heap access.
words.exampleSentence: The OLAP dashboard query on three low-cardinality filter columns (region, category, year) ran in 80 ms after the DBA added a bitmap index — the engine AND-ed three bitmaps in a single pass instead of scanning 500 million rows.
words.etymology: Bitmap from bit (binary digit) + map (a representation); index from Latin indicare. Bitmap indexing for databases was described by O'Neil and Quass in 'Improved Query Performance with Variant Indexes' (1997) and implemented commercially by Oracle and Sybase.

words.shortDefinition: An index on multiple columns; the column order determines which query prefixes it can accelerate.
words.simpleDefinition: A composite index covers multiple columns in a defined order: (a, b, c). The index is sorted first by a, then by b within each a-value, then by c within each (a, b) combination. A query filtering on a, or on a and b, or on all three can use the index. A query filtering only on b or only on c cannot — it violates the leftmost prefix rule.
words.longDefinition: A composite index (also called a multi-column or concatenated index) is a B-tree built over two or more columns, concatenated into a compound key. The index entries are sorted lexicographically: first by the first column, then by the second within each first-column value, and so on. This ordering means the index can only be used efficiently for queries that filter on a prefix of the index columns. A composite index on (last_name, first_name, birth_year) can accelerate: WHERE last_name = 'Smith', WHERE last_name = 'Smith' AND first_name = 'Alice', and WHERE last_name = 'Smith' AND first_name = 'Alice' AND birth_year = 1990. It cannot accelerate WHERE first_name = 'Alice' alone, because first_name values are interleaved across different last_name groups — the index is not sorted by first_name in isolation. Column ordering in a composite index should place the most selective or most frequently filtered column first. However, if a query filters on one column as an equality predicate and range-scans another, the equality column should come first regardless of cardinality, because putting the range column first would limit the index to one seek-and-scan while the equality predicate could have used a more selective path.
words.connector: Think of a composite index like a phone book sorted first by last name, then by first name: you can look up 'Smith, Alice' instantly, but finding all 'Alices' regardless of last name requires reading the entire book.
words.techContext: The leftmost prefix rule is the most common source of 'why isn't my index being used' questions. Always check EXPLAIN to confirm the optimizer is using the expected columns of a composite index and not falling back to a full index scan.
words.exampleSentence: Moving user_id to the first position in the composite index on (created_at, user_id) allowed the 'recent orders by user' query to use the index, cutting scan cost from 2 million rows to 200 rows per lookup.

codeExample.code:
-- Composite index: first column is most selective for equality
CREATE INDEX idx_orders_user_date
  ON orders (user_id, created_at);

-- Uses the full composite index (equality + range):
SELECT * FROM orders
WHERE user_id = 42
  AND created_at > NOW() - INTERVAL '30 days';

-- Cannot use the index (no leading prefix):
SELECT * FROM orders
WHERE created_at > NOW() - INTERVAL '30 days';  -- seq scan

words.etymology: Composite from Latin compositus ('put together'); the term composite index appears in early relational indexing literature and is standard across PostgreSQL, MySQL, Oracle, and SQL Server documentation.

words.shortDefinition: A contiguous run of pages allocated together (e.g., 64 pages = 1 MB in InnoDB) for sequential I/O.
words.simpleDefinition: An extent is a contiguous group of pages that the storage engine allocates together from the OS. When a table grows and needs a new page, the engine allocates a full extent at once — 64 pages (1 MB) in InnoDB. Pages within an extent are adjacent on disk, so reading them in sequence is a single sequential I/O burst rather than dozens of random reads.
words.longDefinition: Pages are the logical unit of database I/O, but allocating them one at a time produces scattered file layouts that degrade sequential scan performance. Extents solve this by pre-allocating contiguous runs of pages. InnoDB uses 64-page extents (1 MB at 16 KB page size); when a table segment needs a new page, InnoDB allocates a full extent, ensuring the next 63 pages are also physically adjacent. A B+ tree range scan that reads pages within the same extent reads them in a single sequential I/O burst — one large read instead of 64 random reads. This is critical on spinning disks (where a seek costs 5–10 ms) and remains important on SSDs (where larger sequential reads are more efficient due to NVMe queue depth and flash erase block alignment). InnoDB organizes tablespace space into segments (one per B-tree index component) and segments into extents. PostgreSQL does not use extents explicitly but benefits from OS-level read-ahead when pages of the same table are physically adjacent. Over time, as page splits and deletes fragment the physical layout, REINDEX (PostgreSQL) or OPTIMIZE TABLE (MySQL) rebuilds the B-tree from scratch, restoring extent locality.
words.connector: Think of an extent like buying a full strip of parking spaces rather than individual spots — when you need to park more cars (store more pages), you can park them in adjacent spaces, making it easy to drive in and out in sequence.
words.techContext: Extent-level allocation is why freshly created indexes have excellent range scan performance that degrades over time as splits scatter pages across extents. REINDEX CONCURRENTLY restores locality without a full table lock.
words.exampleSentence: After REINDEX rebuilt the fragmented orders index, the nightly batch range scan dropped from 8 minutes to 90 seconds because pages now lived in contiguous extents rather than scattered across 200 MB of disk.
words.etymology: Extent from Latin extendere ('to stretch out'), referring to a stretch of contiguous storage. The term is standard in InnoDB's tablespace documentation and in database storage management literature.

words.shortDefinition: A per-relation structure recording how much free space each page has, guiding INSERT placement.
words.simpleDefinition: The free space map is a compact auxiliary data structure that tracks how much free space is available on each heap page. When a new row is inserted, the engine consults the FSM to find a page with enough room rather than scanning every page. In PostgreSQL, the FSM is stored as a separate fork of the relation file.
words.longDefinition: When rows are deleted or updated in a heap file, their slots become available for reuse — but only after VACUUM marks them free and updates the free space map. The FSM is a space-efficient summary structure: PostgreSQL stores the FSM as a binary tree of pages in a separate fork file (with the suffix _fsm). Each leaf of the FSM tree stores a 1-byte representation of the maximum free space in a range of heap pages, supporting O(log N) lookup for a page with at least X bytes free. The FSM is updated by VACUUM (which reclaims dead tuple space) and by the INSERT path (which records remaining free space after a successful insert). Without the FSM, inserting a new row would require scanning heap pages linearly to find space — O(N) for N pages. With the FSM, finding a page with sufficient space is O(log N). The FSM does not track exact free bytes — it stores a quantized approximation (each byte represents free space in units of 32 bytes for an 8 KB page). Visibility Map (VM), a separate fork, records which pages contain only live tuples (no dead tuples) — enabling VACUUM to skip those pages entirely and enabling index-only scans to avoid heap fetches on all-visible pages.
words.connector: Think of the free space map like a seating chart at a restaurant that records which tables have open seats — the host consults it immediately rather than walking through the entire restaurant looking for empty seats.
words.techContext: After a large DELETE or VACUUM, the FSM is updated and subsequent INSERTs immediately reuse the freed space. If autovacuum is not running, the FSM is stale and new inserts extend the table file even though dead space exists — table bloat.
words.exampleSentence: After running VACUUM on the events table, the FSM recorded 12 GB of newly freed space and subsequent batch inserts reused it rather than extending the 40 GB file, keeping storage stable.

codeExample.code:
-- PostgreSQL: inspect free space map usage
SELECT
  pg_size_pretty(pg_relation_size('orders', 'fsm')) AS fsm_size,
  pg_size_pretty(pg_relation_size('orders'))        AS heap_size;

-- Rebuild FSM (useful if autovacuum has been disabled):
VACUUM orders;  -- updates FSM after reclaiming dead tuples

words.etymology: Free space from the physical concept of unoccupied storage; map in the data-structure sense of a mapping from pages to available capacity. The FSM was implemented in PostgreSQL's codebase as a dedicated fork starting with version 8.4.

words.shortDefinition: A replica that applies WAL in real time and can serve read-only queries while staying in sync.
words.simpleDefinition: A hot standby is a replica that is always up-to-date (continuously applying WAL from the primary) and simultaneously available to serve read-only queries. This differs from a warm standby (up-to-date but not queryable) and a cold standby (not continuously receiving WAL). Hot standbys are used for read scaling and fast failover.
words.longDefinition: Hot standby is a PostgreSQL replication mode in which a standby server simultaneously applies incoming WAL records from the primary and accepts read-only SQL connections. The standby runs in 'recovery mode': it replays WAL records to keep its data pages in sync with the primary, while a separate process accepts read connections. Queries on the hot standby see a consistent snapshot taken at the standby's current replay position — slightly behind the primary by the replication lag. Hot standby conflicts can arise when the WAL replay needs to access pages that the standby's read query is currently using (e.g., vacuum on the primary must remove a tuple that a long-running standby query is reading). PostgreSQL resolves conflicts by cancelling the conflicting standby query or waiting for the query to complete (controlled by max_standby_streaming_delay and hot_standby_feedback). Hot standbys are the standard architecture for read scaling in PostgreSQL: the primary handles writes and critical reads; one or more hot standbys absorb read-heavy reporting, analytics, and background jobs. AWS RDS and Aurora both expose hot standby replicas via the same mechanism.
words.connector: Think of a hot standby like a co-pilot who is simultaneously flying the plane on instruments (replaying WAL) and answering passenger questions (serving read queries) — unlike a warm co-pilot who only takes over if the captain incapacitates.
words.techContext: Route time-insensitive reads (analytics, reports, background jobs) to hot standbys to offload the primary. Monitor replication lag with pg_stat_replication.write_lag to ensure standbys are not so far behind that stale reads become a problem.
words.exampleSentence: By routing all reporting queries to the hot standby, we reduced primary CPU utilization from 80% to 35% and eliminated the lock contention between analytical scans and OLTP writes.

codeExample.code:
-- On the hot standby: check replication lag
SELECT
  now() - pg_last_xact_replay_timestamp() AS replication_lag;

-- On the primary: monitor all standbys
SELECT application_name, state,
       write_lag, flush_lag, replay_lag
FROM pg_stat_replication;

words.etymology: Hot standby from aviation terminology: a hot spare is powered on and ready immediately, contrasted with a cold spare (offline). Adopted into database replication nomenclature; hot standby mode was introduced in PostgreSQL 9.0 (2010).

words.shortDefinition: A replication mode where the primary sends WAL records to standbys as they are written, minimizing lag.
words.simpleDefinition: Streaming replication sends WAL records from the primary to standbys in real time over a persistent TCP connection, rather than waiting for full WAL segment files to be shipped. The standby stays within seconds of the primary rather than minutes. It is PostgreSQL's default and most common replication mechanism.
words.longDefinition: PostgreSQL's streaming replication works as follows: on the primary, a WAL sender process accepts a connection from the standby's WAL receiver process. As the primary generates WAL records in pg_wal/, the WAL sender streams them immediately to the standby over the persistent connection. The standby's WAL receiver writes them to its own pg_wal/ and signals the startup process (recovery daemon) to replay them, advancing the standby's data pages. Streaming replication is asynchronous by default: the primary commits when WAL is flushed locally, without waiting for the standby to acknowledge — maximizing primary throughput at the cost of potential data loss of a few WAL records on primary failure. Synchronous replication (synchronous_commit = remote_apply or remote_write) forces the primary to wait for one or more named standbys to acknowledge WAL receipt before confirming commit — eliminating the data-loss window at the cost of added commit latency. Streaming replication can be cascaded: a standby can stream to its own downstream standbys, building a fan-out topology. Replication slots ensure the primary retains WAL until all subscribers have consumed it, preventing lag-induced data loss on slow standbys.
words.connector: Think of streaming replication like a live television broadcast versus tape-delayed programming — the primary is the live broadcast, and the standby receives the signal in real time instead of waiting for an archived tape to arrive hours later.
words.techContext: Monitor streaming replication health via pg_stat_replication on the primary. A growing replay_lag indicates the standby cannot keep up with the primary's WAL generation rate — investigate I/O bottlenecks on the standby or reduce standby query load.
words.exampleSentence: After enabling streaming replication with a synchronous standby in the same availability zone, our RPO dropped from 5 minutes (WAL shipping) to zero committed WAL records, meeting the compliance team's zero-data-loss requirement.

codeExample.code:
# postgresql.conf on primary:
wal_level = replica
max_wal_senders = 5
# Optional: synchronous standby (zero data loss)
synchronous_standby_names = 'standby1'

# pg_hba.conf on primary:
# host replication replicator standby_ip/32 scram-sha-256

# Start standby with pg_basebackup then recovery.conf:
# primary_conninfo = 'host=primary_ip user=replicator'
# recovery_target_timeline = 'latest'

words.etymology: Streaming from the metaphor of a continuous data stream (like a river current); replication from Latin replicare ('to fold back, to repeat'). Streaming replication was introduced in PostgreSQL 9.0 (2010) as an improvement over WAL log shipping.
